title: Identification of a Glycosylation-Related Gene Prognostic Signature for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: PURPOSE: A prognostic signature for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) was developed through identification and integration of glycosylation-related genes (GRGs). METHODS: TCGA RNA-seq data for LUAD and LUSC were analyzed. GRGs were intersected with differentially expressed genes; prognostic GRGs were selected via Cox and LASSO regression to construct a risk model. The immune microenvironment and immunotherapy responses were compared between risk groups. An miRNA-mRNA-transcription factor (TF) network was built and potential drugs were predicted. ADAMTS15 expression was verified by RT-qPCR in NSCLC tissues and cell lines; functional assays (CCK-8, wound healing, Transwell) were performed after ADAMTS15 knockdown in A549 (LUAD) and NCI-H520 (LUSC) cells. RESULTS: A total of 134 differentially expressed GRGs were identified. Ten genes (ADAMTS15, PCSK9, MUC2, B3GNT3, etc.) were selected for the prognostic model, which functioned as an independent prognostic factor. High-risk patients showed poorer immunotherapy response. The regulatory network included 30 TFs and 142 miRNAs, with 107 drug-target pairs predicted. ADAMTS15 was elevated in NSCLC; its knockdown inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion in both LUAD and LUSC cell models. CONCLUSION: A 10-gene prognostic signature derived from GRGs was identified. Functional validation affirmed ADAMTS15's tumor-promoting role, offering insights for NSCLC prognosis and targeted therapy.

title: The potential of PDHA1 as a cuproptosis-related prognostic and immune biomarker in lung squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most common type. Cuproptosis is poorly characterized in lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC). This study evaluated cuproptosis-related genes and the prognostic and biological roles of Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 subunit alpha 1(PDHA1). METHODS: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) transcriptomic/clinical data were analyzed. After PDHA1 overexpression in HCC95 lung adenocarcinoma cells, colony formation, wound healing, flow cytometry, and xenograft assays were performed, including anti-PD-L1-treated groups. RESULTS: PDHA1 was differentially expressed in NSCLC. Higher PDHA1 in LUSC correlated with poorer overall survival (HR = 1.40), supported by GEO trends. PDHA1 correlated with oncogenic/immune pathways, immune infiltration, immunotherapy response in public non-LUSC-specific cohorts, RNA methylation regulators, stemness, genomic alterations, and predicted drug sensitivity. In HCC95 cells, PDHA1 overexpression increased colony formation, wound closure, altered cell-cycle distribution, and xenograft burden. CONCLUSIONS: Higher PDHA1 is associated with adverse prognosis and tumor-related molecular/immune features in LUSC. Experiments support a preliminary tumor-promoting association in an HCC95 model, but immunocompetent models and prospective clinical validation are needed before PDHA1 can be considered a therapeutic or immunotherapy-response biomarker.

title: EXPRESS: Multidomain determinants of perivascular spaces indicate early cerebrovascular vulnerability in individuals at risk of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Perivascular spaces (PVS) are MRI-visible markers of cerebrovascular and glymphatic function, but their regional determinants in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), regarding sex and AD biomarkers, remain poorly understood. METHODS: We studied 1,199 cognitively unimpaired ALFA study participants (aged 54-65 years), genetically enriched for AD risk, with CSF biomarker phenotyping in 296 participants. PVS were automatically quantified in basal ganglia, centrum semiovale, hippocampus, and midbrain on 3T MRI. Counts were modelled using Poisson or negative binomial regression, adjusting for demographics, cardiometabolic, lifestyle, and genetic factors, with effect modification by sex and amyloid/tau (AT) status. RESULTS: PVS showed marked regional specificity. Centrum semiovale PVS were associated with age, male sex, and cardiometabolic factors, whereas hippocampal and midbrain PVS were more closely related to AD biomarker status and sleep or psychological measures. Men exhibited higher centrum semiovale burden while women showed higher counts in hippocampus, midbrain, and basal ganglia. Associations were stronger in amyloid-positive individuals with concurrent tau pathology. Polygenic scores for lipid and metabolic traits contributed modestly to regional PVS variation. CONCLUSIONS: PVS burden is associated with multidomain determinants in preclinical AD with regional, sex-specific, and biomarker-dependent patterns, supporting PVS as accessible MRI markers for risk stratification and precision prevention.
journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism

title: IgG78-Engineered Macrophage Membrane Biomimetic Nanoparticles for Synergistic Targeted Photothermal-Chemotherapy of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
abstract: Clinical management of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) primarily involves non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), and biological agents or gene therapy; however, these treatments have notable limitations. DMARDs, particularly methotrexate (MTX), continue to be the cornerstone of first-line therapy, despite systemic side effects that restrict long-term application and heighten the treatment burden. This study identified elevated levels of CD248 in synovial fibroblasts (RA-FLS) from RA patients, which correlated with increased proliferation and migration. To improve the joint targeting of MTX, a biomimetic nanoplatform was developed using macrophage membrane coating. The anti-CD248 antibody (IgG78) was conjugated to the macrophage membrane surface and incorporated onto mesoporous polydopamine (MPDA) nanoparticles, resulting in active-targeting membrane-coated nanoparticles (MNPs). Experimental results demonstrated that MNPs exhibit exceptional specificity and affinity for RA-FLS. The MTX-loaded MPDA/MTX@M-IgG78 nanosystem showed pronounced therapeutic effects against RA. The high photothermal conversion efficiency of MPDA facilitated controlled MTX release under near-infrared laser irradiation, synergistically enhancing anti-RA efficacy. In conclusion, this innovative biomimetic approach enables targeted MTX delivery to the joints, improving therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing systemic side effects, thereby providing novel strategies for precise RA treatment.

title: From pathophysiology to therapy: dual and triple agonists as a new frontier in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as the most prevalent chronic liver condition worldwide, reflecting the growing global burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D). The complex pathophysiology of MASLD, characterized by insulin resistance (IR), lipotoxicity, and chronic low-grade inflammation, necessitates therapeutic strategies that address systemic metabolic dysfunction rather than isolated hepatic markers. Current evidence highlights the synergistic potential of targeting multiple incretin and metabolic pathways. Dual agonists, most notably Tirzepatide (a GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist), have demonstrated profound efficacy in clinical trials (SURPASS and SURMOUNT programs), achieving significant reductions in hemoglobin A1c, body weight, and liver fat content. Furthermore, dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonists like Survodutide and Cotadutide offer complementary benefits by enhancing energy expenditure and modulating hepatic lipid metabolism. The development of triple agonists, such as Retatrutide (targeting GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors), represents a further escalation in potency, showing unprecedented results in liver fat reduction and weight loss. The integration of these multi-target agents, together with emerging pathways involving amylin analogues and pan-PPAR agonists like Chiglitazar, marks a paradigm shift toward holistic cardiometabolic management. These therapies not only target the resolution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and fibrosis but also address the interconnected risks of cardiovascular and renal complications. This review aims to explore the evolving landscape of pharmacological interventions, focusing on the emergence of dual and triple receptor agonists as a transformative frontier in metabolic dysfunction and MASLD therapy.

title: A nomogram integrating ultrasound features of the primary tumor and axillary lymph nodes with clinicopathological factors to predict high axillary lymph node burden in invasive breast cancer.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and validate a nomogram that integrates ultrasound features of the primary tumor and axillary lymph nodes with lymphovascular invasion (LVI) for early postoperative risk stratification of high axillary nodal burden (HNB; ≥3 positive nodes) in patients with node-positive invasive breast cancer. METHODS: A total of 175 consecutive patients with node-positive invasive breast cancer who underwent surgery between July 2023, and October 2025 were retrospectively included in the development cohort, and an additional 86 patients treated during the same period comprised of the internal validation cohort. Two senior radiologists independently reviewed preoperative ultrasound images and clinicopathological data, including LVI assessed in postoperative surgical specimens. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors and construct the nomogram. RESULTS: The proportions of patients with posterior echo attenuation, microcalcification, claw sign, angular margin sign, spiculation sign (significant long spicules/short spicules), suspicious axillary lymph node status, and lymphovascular invasion were all higher in the high-load group than in the low-load group (all P < 0.05). Multivariate regression analysis showed that the absence of the marginal angular margin sign (OR = 0.190, 95% CI: 0.084 - 0.432, P < 0.001) and the normal axillary lymph node status (OR = 0.208, 95% CI: 0.089 - 0.456, P < 0.001) were independent protective factors for HNB, whereas lymphovascular invasion (presence) (OR = 2.707, 95% CI: 1.363 - 5.377, P = 0.004) was an independent risk factor. ROC analysis showed that the combined detection of marginal angular margin sign, lymph node status, and lymphovascular invasion had a higher AUC value for predicting HNB than individual detections (Z = 4.176, 3.781, and 3.672, respectively; P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: The nomogram incorporating the angular margin sign, axillary lymph node ultrasound status, and LVI provides effective early postoperative risk stratification for HNB in patients with node-positive invasive breast cancer and may facilitate timely adjuvant treatment decision-making.

title: Insights from multi-omics on GLP-1 receptor agonists in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
abstract: Glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the management of T2D and obesity. T2D clustering highlights distinct phenotypes that differ in GLP-1RA benefit. While they have markedly improved quality of life for many individuals, converging evidence indicates that genetic variation, metabolomic remodeling, and gut microbiota composition contribute to substantial inter-individual variability in GLP-1RA efficacy and tolerability. GLP-1RAs, in return, can variably affect the metabolome and microbiome composition in treated individuals. This review focuses on human multi-omics GLP-1RA intervention studies, complemented by relevant mechanistic preclinical evidence. Genetic variation in GLP1R, TCF7L2, and other loci has been associated with differences in glycaemic and weight outcomes, although most findings remain preliminary, inconsistent across populations, or not yet replicated. Pharmacometabolomic studies show recurrent of lipid-related pathways including, glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, ceramides, amino acids, and bile acids, with drug-specific signatures. GLP-1RAs are also associated with changes in gut microbial composition, including taxa such as Akkermansia and Bacteroides, although the direction and clinical significance of these changes vary across studies due to methodological and population heterogeneity. Multi-omics and AI-based models show promise for predicting treatment response by integrating genetic, metabolic, microbial, and clinical data to supporting more effective and individualized therapy and advancing precision medicine.

title: Microtube-Assisted Paraffin Embedding and Sectioning of Fragile 3D Tumor Spheroids for High-Quality Histology.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) spheroid models have become essential in cancer biology, drug screening, and tissue engineering. However, their small size, fragile structure, and tendency to disintegrate during routine histoprocessing present persistent technical challenges. Conventional paraffin embedding often results in tissue fragmentation, loss of spatial orientation, and poor section quality, whereas cryosectioning often compromises cellular morphology. Here, we present a robust, cost-effective protocol for preserving and sectioning fragile 3D spheroids, resulting in high-quality histological sections with intact architecture and excellent cellular detail. The method involves optimized handling and embedding procedures that stabilize spheroids during standard formalin fixation, paraffin infiltration, and microtomy, eliminating mechanical distortion and preserving spherical integrity for consistent sectioning. We demonstrate the successful application of this protocol across different tumor spheroids derived from distinct tissue types, including MDA-MB-231 (breast carcinoma), Caco-2 (colorectal adenocarcinoma), and A549 (lung carcinoma) cell lines, with subsequent compatibility with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining protocols. This protocol is compatible with immunohistochemistry (IHC) and immunofluorescence (IF). In our qualitative comparison with conventional methods, we found that our approach effectively limits sample loss, promotes consistent inter-section reproducibility, and preserves fine structural features, such as necrotic cores, proliferative zones, and extracellular matrix components. This protocol provides a reliable, accessible solution for routine histological analysis of fragile 3D spheroids, facilitating more accurate morphological assessment in translational research settings. Key features • Cost-effective agarose-coated plates for reproducible spheroid formation. • Complete in-tube processing to minimize sample loss and damage. • Floating tube system for reliable paraffin infiltration without specialized equipment. • Produces high-quality sections compatible with H&E. Graphical overview.

title: Deep brain stimulation in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a well-established treatment for neurological disorders, but its efficacy and safety in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain uncertain. This narrative review synthesizes nine clinical trials in patients with mild to severe AD, focusing on stimulation of the fornix, nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM), and ventral capsule/ventral striatum. Literature was identified through PubMed using the terms "deep brain stimulation" and "Alzheimer's disease," and the results were restricted to clinical trials and case reports in English, with additional references identified through Google Scholar. Across studies, DBS was safe and well tolerated, with few adverse events. Stimulation produced short-term cognitive improvements, most commonly measured by Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale cognitive subscale, along with transient reversal of glucose hypometabolism and activation of memory-related networks. One study reported slowed hippocampal atrophy, suggesting neuroplastic effects. In severe AD, DBS targeting both the fornix and NBM yielded transient cognitive gains, with NBM-DBS showing greater benefit for neuropsychiatric symptoms and caregiver burden. Patients with higher baseline cognition and glucose metabolism responded more favorably to DBS. Age-related differences emerged: younger patients (<65 years old), with earlier onset and more aggressive progression, showed less favorable responses to DBS targeting the fornix, whereas older patients (≥65 years old) had comparatively better outcomes. Despite these benefits, DBS does not halt disease progression or reverse AD pathology. Larger, biomarker-stratified, sham-controlled trials with extended follow-up are needed to clarify durability, identify optimal patient subgroups, and determine the most effective stimulation targets.

title: HistoBreastCAD: an integrated deep learning framework for segmentation and multiclass classification of whole-slide breast histopathology images.
abstract: Breast cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, and histopathological examination remains the diagnostic gold standard. This study presents HistoBreastCAD, an integrated deep learning framework that combines tissue-region segmentation, four-class histopathology classification, spatial mapping of predictions, and interactive whole-slide image (WSI) review. Segmentation was evaluated using WSI-grouped five-fold cross-validation, while classification used source-image-grouped five-fold cross-validation to prevent source-level data leakage. The final DeepLabV3+ L0 segmentation configuration achieved an out-of-fold micro-Dice of 0.8390, IoU of 0.7226, precision of 0.8278, and recall of 0.8505. For classification, EfficientNetB0 was the strongest individual model, while a frozen equal-weight soft-voting ensemble of EfficientNetB0 and ResNet18-GAP-attention achieved an accuracy of 0.8283 ± 0.0320 and macro-F1 of 0.8282 ± 0.0316, outperforming EfficientNetB0 in all five validation folds. An exploratory reader study using the 100 microscopy images from the held-out BACH test set showed moderate interobserver agreement between two pathologists (Cohen's κ = 0.5105; n = 95), whereas model-to-reader concordance was lower. The ensemble did not increase reader concordance relative to EfficientNetB0. HistoBreastCAD therefore demonstrates the feasibility of integrating established deep learning components into a source-separated WSI-oriented digital pathology workflow. However, external multi-institutional validation, adjudicated reader studies, and formal explainability assessment are required before claims of clinical generalizability or utility can be supported.

title: PP2A targeting: balancing anticancer potential and neurological risk.
abstract: Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a multifunctional serine/threonine phosphatase that regulates cell-cycle progression, oncogenic signaling, neuronal development, synaptic homeostasis, and protein proteostasis. Its dysregulation contributes to cancer, whereas impaired PP2A activity in the nervous system is linked to neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegenerative proteinopathies, including tau and α-synuclein pathology. These divergent roles create both opportunities and safety challenges for PP2A-directed therapies. This review examines PP2A as a modular holoenzyme system whose subunit composition determines substrate specificity and context-dependent biological effects. We discuss PP2A dysfunction in cancer, including genetic and regulatory alterations affecting PP2A subunits, assembly, and endogenous inhibitors, and compare therapeutic PP2A activation with transient inhibition. The latter approach is exemplified by LB100, which sensitizes treatment-stressed tumor cells to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immunotherapy by disrupting checkpoint adaptation and stress recovery. We further evaluate the neurological implications of systemic phosphatase inhibition, LB100 conversion to the active metabolite endothall, clinical safety and pharmacokinetic data, and the limited brain-tumor penetration of intact LB100. We propose that the clinical utility of PP2A inhibition depends on defining a therapeutic corridor that integrates dosing schedule, parent-drug and metabolite exposure, tumor target engagement, biomarker-informed patient selection, and preservation of PP2A-dependent homeostasis in normal tissues, particularly the nervous system.
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

title: A CD68-expressing tissue-homing subset in peripheral CD8+ T cells predicts response to anti-PD-1 therapy in lung cancer.
abstract: BACKGROUND: T-cell function is regulated by immunometabolism, and lysosomes are signaling hubs. CD68 (LAMP4), traditionally regarded as a monocyte/macrophage marker, has been largely neglected in T cell biology. We aimed to assess the link between CD68 expression in T cells and anti-PD-1 response in lung cancer, and its potential as an early dynamic biomarker in peripheral blood CD8+ T cells. METHODS: We analyzed transcriptomic (GSE126044, GSE135222, GSE166449) and single-cell (GSE207422) data from anti-PD-1-treated lung cancer cohorts to identify lysosome related pathways and key genes, validated with peripheral blood CD8+ T cell data (GSE111414). Prospectively, we enrolled lung cancer patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy, collecting peripheral blood at baseline and week 3. Flow cytometry measured CD68 in CD8+ T cells and subsets, assessing association with response, progression-free survival (PFS), and functional markers (granzyme B, perforin, Ki-67, CD69, IFN-γ, IL-1β). RESULTS: Responders showed enrichment of lysosome pathways and upregulation of 8 lysosome related genes including CD68, positively correlated with monocyte and T cell infiltration. Single-cell data linked CD68 expression in T cell to favorable response. After one cycle, the proportion of CD8+CD68+ T cells was lower in non-responders (P<0.05), with AUC 0.803 (P=0.044) and cutoff 1.015%, stratifying PFS (P=0.0225). CD68 was highest in naïve T cells at baseline, but decreased across subsets after treatment in non-responders (all P<0.01). Functionally, compared with CD8+CD68- T cells, CD8+CD68+ T cells exhibited lower expression of granzyme B and perforin but higher expression of Ki-67, CD69, IFN-γ, and IL-1β (all P<0.001), suggesting a CD8+ T cell state characterized by lower cytotoxicity and enhanced proliferative and cytokine producing capacities, accompanied by a tissue residency associated phenotype. CONCLUSION: CD8+CD68+ T cells exhibit lower cytotoxicity but greater proliferative and cytokine producing capacities, together with a tissue residency associated phenotype, suggesting a precursor-like state. Low CD68 expression in tumor-infiltrating T cells and the post-treatment reduction of CD68 expression in peripheral blood CD8+ T cells are associated with resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy in lung cancer. These findings suggest that CD8+CD68+ T cells may serve as a potential early dynamic immune biomarker for monitoring and assessing response to anti-PD-1 therapy in lung cancer.

title: Impact of Chile's Explicit Health Guarantees Policy on breast cancer mortality: an interrupted time series analysis (1990-2024).
abstract: BACKGROUND: Breast cancer mortality in Chile has shown divergent trends over recent decades, with declining age-adjusted rates alongside increasing crude mortality driven by population aging. In 2005, Chile incorporated breast cancer into the Explicit Health Guarantees Regime (AUGE/GES), ensuring universal access, timeliness, quality standards, and financial protection across the continuum of care. Whether this policy produced an independent, detectable impact on population-level breast cancer mortality remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted an interrupted time series (ITS) analysis of female breast cancer mortality in Chile from 1990 to 2024. Annual death counts were obtained from national vital statistics and modeled using negative binomial regression with population offsets. Age-standardized mortality rates were calculated using the 2017 Chilean population as the reference. ITS models estimated changes in level and slope associated with two intervention points: the consolidation of the National Breast Cancer Program in 1995 and the implementation of AUGE/GES in 2005. Analyses were performed for the total female population and by age group. RESULTS: While the absolute number of deaths and crude mortality rates increased over time, age-standardized breast cancer mortality declined steadily throughout the study period. A significant change in trend was observed after 1995, consistent with the early programmatic organization of breast cancer services. In contrast, no additional statistically significant change in level or slope was detected after 2005 at the population level or among women aged ≥40/≥50 years. Age-stratified analyses revealed a more pronounced post-2005 decline among women aged 65-69 and ≥80 years, suggesting age- and cohort-specific effects. CONCLUSIONS: Breast cancer mortality risk in Chile has declined primarily due to long-term secular trends and early programmatic strengthening, while population aging has driven increasing crude mortality. The AUGE/GES reform has consolidated access and financial protection, with heterogeneous benefits in older cohorts, but without generating a detectable additional inflection in national mortality trends. Further mortality reductions will require integrated, equity-oriented strategies emphasizing organized screening, timely diagnosis, and high-quality treatment across the life course.

title: Breast health information, motivation, behavioral skills, and breast self-examination behavior among female medical college students: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Based on the Information-Motivation-Behavioral Skills Model (IMB), this study examined differences in breast cancer (BC) prevention knowledge, perceived barriers, self-efficacy, and breast self-examination (BSE) practices between female nursing and pharmacy students. We hypothesized that nursing students would demonstrate more favorable IMB profiles and that the association between academic major and BSE behavior would be statistically explained by these constructs. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 997 female nursing and pharmacy students from a medical college (May-June 2026). Data were collected using the Champion Health Belief Model Scale (CHBMS) and a self-developed BC knowledge questionnaire. Multivariate logistic regression identified factors associated with BSE behavior, adjusting for grade, residence, and family history. Analyses were performed using SPSS 20.0 (α = 0.05). RESULTS: Compared with pharmacy students, nursing students exhibited significantly higher knowledge scores (7.21 ± 2.51 vs. 6.05 ± 2.89, t = 6.21, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.43), self-efficacy scores (3.35 ± 0.72 vs. 3.18 ± 0.79, t = 3.54, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.22), and BSE rates (60.6% vs. 32.0%, χ2 = 81.07, p < 0.001), with small to moderate effect sizes. Nursing students also reported lower perceived barrier scores (2.65 ± 0.78 vs. 2.95 ± 0.85, t = -6.04, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.37). Multivariate logistic regression identified prior breast health education (OR = 4.642, 95% CI: 3.231-6.670, p < 0.001) and higher self-efficacy (OR = 1.817, 95% CI: 1.453-2.272, p < 0.001) as independent predictors of BSE, while higher perceived barriers were associated with lower odds of BSE (OR = 0.286, 95% CI: 0.226-0.360, p < 0.001). After adjusting for these IMB constructs, the OR for nursing major decreased from 1.912 to 1.648, suggesting that these factors partially explain the inter-major difference in BSE behavior. CONCLUSION: In this cross-sectional study, nursing students demonstrated higher BC prevention literacy than pharmacy students. Higher self-efficacy and lower perceived barriers, but not knowledge, were independently associated with BSE. These findings suggest that breast health education in medical colleges should prioritize skills training and barrier reduction over knowledge transfer alone.

title: Practice patterns and outcomes of local and systemic therapy for single-site metastatic non-small cell lung cancer in the era of immunotherapy.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Prognosis of lung cancer with single metastatic sites in the era of immunotherapy remains poorly described. We used the National Cancer Database to assess how metastatic site and the use of local therapy with systemic immunotherapy is associated with prognosis in the United States. METHODS: Patients with clinical stage IVA lung cancer treated with immunotherapy were identified in the National Cancer Database (2018-2023). Patients were stratified by metastatic site and treatment: systemic immunotherapy with or without local therapy (immunotherapy + local therapy or immunotherapy). Prognosis was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox survival analysis landmarked at median time from diagnosis to local therapy. RESULTS: Among included patients (N = 20,214), metastases included lung (N = 5308; 26.3%), brain (N = 3516; 17.4%), bone (N = 3142; 15.5%), distant lymph node (N = 1219; 6.0%), liver (N = 874; 4.3%), and other metastases (N = 6155; 30.4%). A total of 13,890 patients (68.7%) were treated with immunotherapy, and 6324 patients (31.3%) were treated with immunotherapy + local therapy (70.2% received chemotherapy, 27.2% radiation, and 9.8% surgery). Poor 5-year overall survival was associated with bone (20.9%) and liver (15.9%) metastases compared with brain (33.4%). Five-year survival was greater in patients selected for local therapy (30.3% vs 20.5%, P < .001); thoracic and extrathoracic local therapy was associated with greater overall survival compared with extrathoracic local therapy alone (37.7% vs 28.2%, P < .001). Differences in 5-year survival with local therapy varied by metastatic site (10.4% lung, 7.1% brain, 0.1% liver). CONCLUSIONS: The addition of local therapy to a systemic regimen containing immunotherapy was common for patients with single metastatic sites. Patients selected for local therapy had a more favorable prognosis, which varied by metastatic site.

title: Hormone receptor-positive adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast with cross-modality imaging discrepancy: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Primary adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast (ACCB) is a rare salivary gland-type malignancy characterized by biphasic luminal epithelial and myoepithelial/basal differentiation. Although most ACCBs exhibit a triple-negative phenotype, hormone receptor-positive tumors occur, and evidence guiding endocrine therapy is limited. A 42-year-old woman presented with a gradually enlarging right breast mass. Ultrasonography and MRI were suspicious for malignancy (BI-RADS 4B and BI-RADS MRI category 5), whereas diagnostic mammography showed focal increased glandular density (BI-RADS 0) and benign punctate calcifications (BI-RADS 2). Core needle biopsy showed cribriform architecture, and immunohistochemistry demonstrated expression of CK7, CD117, and p63, supporting a diagnosis of ACCB. The biopsy showed estrogen receptor expression in 10%-20% of tumor cells, progesterone receptor expression in approximately 5%, and a HER2 score of 0. The patient underwent right mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy. The resection specimen confirmed a 3.0 cm ACCB with predominantly cribriform architecture and additional solid growth, with ER and PR each expressed in approximately 30% of tumor cells, a HER2 IHC score of 0, and a negative sentinel lymph node [pT2 pN0(sn)]. She completed 5 years of adjuvant tamoxifen therapy. At the last follow-up, approximately 73 months after surgery, no local, regional, or distant recurrence was detected. This case highlights the value of integrating histomorphology and immunohistochemical findings when imaging findings differ across modalities and illustrates the immunophenotypic heterogeneity of ACCB. The recurrence-free outcome provides additional follow-up information for hormone receptor-positive ACCB but cannot establish benefit from endocrine therapy; individualized treatment and long-term surveillance remain warranted.

title: Editorial: Community series in unveiling the next generation of cancer immunity & immunotherapy in lung cancer, volume II.
Perspectives on plasma biomarkers for point-of-care diagnostics in Alzheimer's disease: Insights into 2D-BioPAD.
abstract: We investigated the potential of plasma biomarkers for point-of-care in vitro diagnostics in Alzheimer's disease by collecting insights from 99 stakeholders primarily from Greece, including patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals, and researchers. Data from an online survey was analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Key biomarkers reported by participants included Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, pTau217, and neurofilament light chain. While biomarkers were recognized for their value in prognosis, diagnosis, and monitoring, most participants were unfamiliar with point-of-care in vitro diagnostics. Major concerns regarding implementation included cost, reimbursement, and accessibility, underscoring the need for more feasible and context-appropriate diagnostic solutions.

title: Heterogeneous progression of AT(N) biomarkers in data-driven subtypes of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity in brain atrophy patterns and progression rates. Data-driven subtyping based on the Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) model has identified distinct MRI-derived subtypes, but the longitudinal dynamics of these subtypes within the AT(N) framework remain unknown. METHODS: This study included 1,576 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) with at least two visits. SuStaIn was applied to volumetric measurements of 11 brain regions to identify imaging-based subtypes. Within each subtype, we fitted a Bayesian latent time longitudinal joint mixed-effects model incorporating six biomarkers: amyloid PET (A), CSF p-tau (T), hippocampal volume, cingulate volume, thalamic volume (N), and ADAS-Cog13 (X), with APOE ε4 as a covariate. RESULTS: The three subtypes exhibited distinctly different longitudinal patterns. Subtype 1 showed early elevation of amyloid, followed by a sharp decline in hippocampal volume, which was tightly coupled with cognitive deterioration. Subtype 2 featured early involvement of cortical regions such as the cingulate cortex, with hippocampal changes occurring at a similar timing to Subtype 1 but accompanied by earlier cortical and thalamic involvement. Subtype 3 exhibited early rapid hippocampal atrophy that later plateaued, and demonstrated the strongest hippocampus-cognition coupling. The association of APOE ε4 with biomarker trajectories was subtype-dependent: its effect estimates were largest for amyloid and p-tau in Subtype 1, whereas in Subtype 3 the effect estimates were significant for nearly all biomarkers, with the largest estimate for cognition. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that AD subtypes defined by spatial atrophy patterns also differ fundamentally in temporal biomarker dynamics and APOE ε4 association, supporting subtype-stratified modeling of disease progression.

title: From recanalization to recovery: inflammation and futile reperfusion after mechanical thrombectomy.
abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has markedly improved reperfusion outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by large-vessel occlusion. However, successful angiographic reperfusion does not invariably translate into functional independence. Poor functional outcome despite successful angiographic reperfusion is commonly described as futile reperfusion. This clinical-angiographic mismatch may reflect persistent tissue injury, including inflammatory injury, alongside pretreatment damage and other determinants of outcome. Experimental findings and clinical associations implicate persistent inflammatory activation, thrombo-inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, microvascular no-reflow, and blood-brain barrier disruption as contributors to secondary tissue injury after MT. Here, we examine potential inflammatory contributions to futile reperfusion and consider how inflammatory biomarkers might inform risk stratification after MT. Ischemia activates microglia, endothelial cells, platelets, complement pathways, and circulating immune cells. Subsequent reperfusion may amplify oxidative stress, cytokine signaling, neutrophil-endothelial interactions, neutrophil extracellular trap formation, matrix metalloproteinase activity, and barrier failure. Together, these processes can promote microvascular obstruction, cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, infarct growth, and impaired neurological recovery despite successful angiographic reperfusion. Among circulating biomarkers, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio has been studied repeatedly, alongside platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, systemic immune-inflammation index, systemic inflammation response index, interleukin-6, matrix metalloproteinase-9, and other molecular markers. Their specificity, incremental predictive value, and clinical utility require further validation in standardized thrombectomy cohorts. We therefore view inflammation as a plausible biological link between macrovascular reperfusion and persistent tissue-level injury after MT. From a translational perspective, the immediate priorities are to standardize sampling protocols, characterize dynamic inflammatory trajectories, develop multimodal prediction models, and test biomarker-guided therapeutic strategies.

title: Emerging roles of apolipoprotein E4 in cerebral small vessel disease-related cognitive impairment: mechanistic insights and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a major contributor to cognitive decline and vascular cognitive impairment in the elderly. However, the extent to which apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) contributes to sporadic, non-amyloid CSVD remains unclear. Previous literature has often inferred CSVD mechanisms from Alzheimer's disease (AD) research, carrying the risk of overstating disease-specific causal relationships. Therefore, this narrative review re-evaluates the relationship between ApoE4 and CSVD using a CSVD-centric hierarchy of evidence. Population-based imaging and epidemiological data suggest that "APOE" ε4 may alter susceptibility to white matter injury and cognitive impairment; however, the effect sizes are generally small or context-dependent, and associations are influenced by factors such as age, hypertension, diabetes, total vascular risk burden, AD pathology, ancestry, sex, and "APOE" gene dosage. Evidence is stronger for cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA)-which involves mechanisms distinct from sporadic arteriolosclerotic CSVD-and thus warrants separate discussion. At the mechanistic level, direct evidence regarding CSVD supports endothelial dysfunction, BBB leakage, neurovascular unit (NVU) instability, and white matter injury as core pathological processes. Among the evidence specific to ApoE4, models involving impaired neurovascular regulation and chronic hypoperfusion are the most compelling; conversely, mechanisms such as the cyclophilin A-MMP-9 pathway, TREM2-ApoE signaling, insulin receptor trafficking, reelin-related synaptic effects, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and autophagy currently rely primarily on AD research or preclinical evidence. Two recently proposed specific hypotheses-the brain-heart-kidney axis hypothesis and the microglial lipid droplet model-offer valuable conceptual frameworks but should be viewed as testable theories rather than established mechanisms. To date, no ApoE4-targeted therapies have been proven effective for CSVD-related cognitive impairment future research should prioritize genotype-stratified longitudinal CSVD cohorts, standardized imaging studies, adjustment for Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers, analysis of interactions between vascular risk factors, studies on human white matter tissue, and the development of ApoE4 disease models that integrate chronic hypoperfusion and vascular comorbidities.

title: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy in geriatric patients with non-small cell lung cancer: A real-world analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has been shown to significantly improve survival in patients with stage IB-IIIB non-small cell lung cancer. However, it is unknown whether geriatric patients experience similar benefits. Using a large national cohort, we studied outcomes of neoadjuvant immunotherapy in geriatric patients with stage IB-IIIB non-small cell lung cancer. METHODS: Patients with stage IB-IIIB non-small cell lung cancer treated over 24 months (2022-2023) were identified in the National Cancer Database. Geriatric patients were defined as being older than 75 years. Geriatric patients and younger patients aged 75 years or less were compared in terms of treatment intensity, perioperative outcomes, and survival. Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards models were used for statistical analysis of survival. Multivariable logistic regression was used to analyze perioperative outcomes. RESULTS: 21,070 patients aged more than 75 years with clinical stage IB-IIIB non-small cell lung cancer were included in this analysis. Among them, 4467 (21.2%) received surgery and 447 (10.0%) received neoadjuvant immunotherapy, compared with 35.3% and 17.9% of younger patients, respectively (P < .001). Both surgery (adjusted HR 0.34 [0.27-0.43], P < .001) and neoadjuvant immunotherapy (0.39 [0.25-0.63], P < .001) were associated with improved survival in geriatric patients. Geriatric patients who received neoadjuvant immunotherapy also demonstrated acceptable perioperative outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: In a large national cohort, we show that although geriatric patients have lower treatment intensity than younger patients, both surgery and neoadjuvant immunotherapy render a survival benefit while retaining acceptable perioperative outcomes. Whenever possible, standard of care treatment should be pursued in geriatric patients, and age in isolation should not exclude patients from optimal treatments.

title: Is pneumonectomy appropriate after chemoimmunotherapy? Outcomes of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy followed by pneumonectomy in the United States.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The appropriateness of pneumonectomy for non-small cell lung cancer after neoadjuvant therapy is not well characterized, and there is concern for substantially greater mortality on the basis of results of trials such as Intergroup-0139. Here, we present current use and outcomes of pneumonectomy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. METHODS: Using the National Cancer Database, we identified and included adults with clinical stage I-III lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma who were diagnosed between 2018 and 2023 and treated with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy followed by lobectomy or pneumonectomy. Three-year overall survival was assessed by Kaplan-Meier. Propensity matching and Cox proportional hazards models were based on patient and tumor characteristics. RESULTS: The study included 2703 (94%) lobectomies and 173 (6%) pneumonectomies. Patients who underwent pneumonectomy had a more advanced T stage (64% vs 47% T3+, P < .001) but a lower comorbidity burden (71% vs 58% Charlson-Deyo of 0, P = .01). They had greater rates of 30-day unplanned readmission (9% vs 4%, P = .001) and R1+ resection (7.1% vs 3.9%, P = .046) but comparable 90-day mortality (<4.5% vs 2%, P = .24). Unadjusted 3-year overall survival was not significantly different between the 2 groups: 80% for pneumonectomy and 82% for lobectomy (P = .08). Similar trends were observed after propensity-matching for patient and tumor characteristics: 79% for pneumonectomy and 78% for lobectomy (P = .19). On Cox models, pneumonectomy was associated with a greater hazard ratio of mortality, but this was not statistically significant (odds ratio, 1.56; 95% CI, 0.91-2.68; P = .09). CONCLUSIONS: Pneumonectomy after induction chemoimmunotherapy demonstrated comparable early survival with lobectomy among selected patients in the United States. Use of pneumonectomy after chemoimmunotherapy in appropriate candidates appears reasonable.

title: Pancreatic and Gallbladder Adverse Events Associated with Tirzepatide in Obesity Management: A Scoping Review.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity is a chronic and relapsing condition that affects all demographics and results in comorbidities, rising healthcare costs, and social challenges. Tirzepatide, a novel dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, has emerged as a promising therapy offering significant weight reduction. However, uncertainty remains regarding its pancreatic and gallbladder safety profile across different populations and evidence sources. AIM: To systematically map existing evidence on the safety of tirzepatide in obesity management, with an emphasis on pancreatic- and gallbladder-related adverse events (AEs) across randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, case reports, and pharmacovigilance evidence. METHODS: Following the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), expanded with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, this scoping review included RCTs, observational studies, and post-marketing safety reports identified between December 2019 and September 2025. The searches were conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), with additional evidence identified through gray literature, targeted journal searches, and published pharmacovigilance studies based on the EudraVigilance database. ClinicalTrials.gov was subsequently searched as an additional source to identify relevant clinical trials. Studies were eligible if they examined pancreatic or gallbladder AEs in the context of tirzepatide exposure among individuals with obesity. The review included 11 RCTs, 5 observational studies, 4 case reports, 1 EudraVigilance pharmacovigilance analysis, and 575 FAERS reports. Pancreatic and gallbladder AEs were systematically extracted and coded using MedDRA version 28.1, following the predetermined hierarchy. Findings were mapped descriptively across data sources without formal comparative statistical testing. RESULTS: Pancreatic and gallbladder AEs were reported infrequently in RCTs. Pancreatitis was reported in 11 participants across five RCTs, with study-specific frequencies ranging from 0.2% (3 of 1,896) to 3.7% (1 of 27), while cholelithiasis was reported in 73 participants across 11 RCTs, with frequencies ranging from 0.3% (1 of 335 and 1 of 364) to 3.7% (1 of 27). Among observational studies, pancreatitis was reported in three studies, with proportions of 0.6% (63/10,002), 0.9% (1/110), and 2.1% (5,882/280,094). One retrospective cohort study reported an incidence rate of 3.84 events per 1,000 person-years among 9,193 participants, while cholelithiasis was reported at 11.89 events per 1,000 person-years in the same cohort. In the EudraVigilance pharmacovigilance analysis, pancreatitis represented 363 reported AEs (6.3% of all AEs and 19.4% of gastrointestinal AEs). In the FAERS database, pancreatitis accounted for 155/288 pancreatic-related reports [53.8%] and cholelithiasis for 143/249 gallbladder-related reports [57.4%]. Four case reports described six distinct AEs: edematous pancreatitis, acute pancreatitis, pancreatitis necrotizing, acalculous cholecystitis, gallstones, and gallbladder wall thickening, each reported once. Female participants, White participants, adults aged 18-64 years, and participants from the United States (US) predominated among reported demographic characteristics; however, demographic characteristics and comorbidity profiles were inconsistently reported and varied across studies. CONCLUSION: Pancreatic and gallbladder AEs were reported across clinical trials, observational studies, case reports, and pharmacovigilance databases. RCTs generally reported low frequencies of pancreatobiliary AEs, whereas pharmacovigilance databases captured a broader spectrum of reported events. Variability in study populations, comorbidity profiles, reporting methods, and the absence of exposure denominators limited direct comparison across evidence sources. Vigilant monitoring and standardized AE reporting are needed to further characterize the pancreatobiliary safety profile of tirzepatide.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy

title: The Impact of Incretin-Based Therapies on Anthropometric and Metabolic Parameters in Women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), recently renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), affects 170 million women globally and is often accompanied by obesity and various levels of insulin resistance. Incretin-based therapies, including the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists liraglutide and semaglutide, and the dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) agonist tirzepatide, offer a biologically plausible mechanism for targeting metabolic dysfunction in PMOS. This review examines clinical trial evidence on the anthropometric and metabolic effects of incretin-based therapies in this population, including a focus on women of reproductive age, who face distinct challenges related to preconception planning, treatment duration, and post-discontinuation metabolic and weight management. Available literature shows that liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide produce clinically meaningful reductions in body weight, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference, with some studies also confirming preferential effects on visceral and ectopic fat compartments. Glycaemic and insulin resistance outcomes vary across studies, while lipid and blood pressure effects remain incompletely characterized. Although emerging data suggest that higher-potency agents may yield more consistent weight-loss benefits, available PMOS-specific evidence does not establish comparative metabolic superiority among agents. Interpretation of the available evidence is limited by the predominance of short-term trials at sub-obesity doses, frequent co-administration with metformin, and the absence of phenotype-stratified data, leaving the full metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS incompletely defined. Larger, longer, and higher-dose trials are needed to fully characterize the anthropometric and metabolic potential of these agents in PMOS.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy

title: Application of computational methods in the drug discovery and development of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to cognitive decline. As the most common dementia, AD affects over 50 million individuals worldwide, with 10 million new cases each year. Despite many significant progresses in AD research fields, there is still no effective treatment. Advances in molecular modelling and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm have facilitated the application of computational methods in AD drug development, offering advantages in terms of efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and resource conservation. These strategies, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, and de novo drug design, have been widely employed in the past decades. Additionally, AI pharmaceutical companies have revolutionized the traditional drug development pipeline such as AD biomarker discovery, accurate diagnosis and precision medicine, etc. This review offers a thorough summary of recent progresses in computational-based methodologies in the study of AD drug development, including the elucidation the pathological mechanism at the molecular level, target identification, target 3D structure prediction, lead compound discovery, de novo molecular generation, multi-target directed ligands, drug repurposing, biomarker discovery, etc., showing promising applications of molecular modelling and AI in the development of AD therapy.

title: Systemic Glucose-Lowering Therapies and Periodontal and Peri-Implant Outcomes in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and periodontitis are bidirectionally linked. Systemic glucose-lowering drug classes differ in their extra-glycaemic effects on inflammation and bone, which could plausibly modify periodontal and peri-implant health; however, this evidence has not been synthesised across drug classes. We conducted a systematic review and evidence gap map (EGM), with sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors examined as a pre-specified evidence gap. PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science, and Scopus were searched and cross-checked against the Consensus academic corpus. Eligible studies enrolled adults with T2DM, evaluated a systemic glucose-lowering drug as the exposure, and reported a periodontal or peri-implant outcome. Studies of local drug delivery and periodontal therapy aimed at improving glycaemic control were excluded from the systematic-review layer; all study designs, including preclinical studies, were charted in the EGM. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias 2 (RoB 2) tool and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Four studies were included: one randomised controlled trial and three observational studies. These comprised a trial of a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor (sitagliptin) added to metformin, which reported improvements in probing depth, clinical attachment level, bleeding on probing, and alveolar bone density; a cohort study comparing peri-implant marginal bone loss among users of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 receptor agonists), metformin, and insulin, with the least bone loss observed among glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist users; a large pharmacoepidemiological cohort evaluating DPP-4 inhibitor exposure; and a cross-sectional survey of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist users. Meta-analysis was not feasible because of substantial heterogeneity. The EGM, comprising eight drug classes and six outcome domains, showed that evidence was concentrated in glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and metformin and was almost entirely preclinical; the only high-level evidence cell was represented by a single DPP-4 inhibitor randomised controlled trial, while SGLT2 inhibitors constituted a complete evidence gap across all outcome domains. Based on the four included studies, human evidence linking systemic glucose-lowering therapy with periodontal outcomes in adults with T2DM is sparse, heterogeneous, and of low certainty, with weak signals favouring incretin-based therapies. SGLT2 inhibitors remain entirely unstudied in this context despite biological plausibility. The EGM identifies specific, high-value priorities for future randomised trials and prospective cohort studies.

title: Integrating cure and care in Alzheimer's disease: a systems perspective for precision medicine.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease remains a major global health challenge, with limited disease-modifying therapies and a rapidly growing societal burden. Although amyloid and tau remain central to the field, current evidence also implicates neuroinflammation, immune dysregulation, vascular dysfunction, and host-microbe interactions in disease pathogenesis. These developments support a broader systems framework, but simply combining additional disciplines or data modalities does not by itself preserve the dynamic biology or lived experience of disease. Artificial intelligence multi-omics, and digital biomarkers can help identify clinically meaningful patterns only when data and models preserve relevant structure across time, scale, context, and uncertainty. Realizing this potential will require responsible international data sharing, interoperable infrastructure, explicit evidence provenance, and ethical governance grounded in FAIR principles, context-appropriate explainability, and privacy-preserving approaches such as federated learning. Scientific progress should therefore be measured not only by disease modification, but also by patterns of cognition, behavior, function, quality of life, and caregiver burden. This Perspective argues that cure and care are not competing or merely parallel priorities; they are linked outputs of the same continuously learning research and care ecosystem.

title: Current Status and Treatment Outcomes of Mechanical Thrombectomy for Acute Large Vessel Occlusion during On- and Off-Hours in Our Institution.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is the standard of care for acute large vessel occlusion (LVO); however, off-hours treatment may be delayed because of limited staffing. We compared MT outcomes between on-hours and off-hours at a single center and investigated factors associated with 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-3. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 101 consecutive patients with anterior circulation LVO and a pre-stroke mRS 0-2 who underwent MT at Tokorozawa Central Hospital between January 2020 and December 2025. Patients were classified into on-hours (9:00-17:00 on Mondays through Saturdays, excluding national holidays and the period from December 31 to January 3) and off-hours groups based on hospital arrival time. The primary endpoint was 90-day mRS 0-3. Secondary endpoints included Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction (TICI) grade 2b-3, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), and any intracranial hemorrhage. Time metrics, including onset-to-door time (ODT), door-to-image time, door-to-needle time, image-to-puncture time (IPT), door-to-puncture time (DPT), puncture-to-recanalization time (PRT), door-to-recanalization time (DRT), and onset-to-recanalization time (ORT), were compared between the 2 groups, and factors associated with 90-day mRS 0-3 were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses. RESULTS: The on-hours group comprised 46 patients and the off-hours group 55 patients. Compared with the on-hours group, the off-hours group had significantly longer IPT (median 83 vs. 51 min, p <0.001), DPT (median 103 vs. 71 min, p <0.001), and DRT (median 151 vs. 124 min, p = 0.003). ODT and ORT did not differ significantly between the groups (median 105 vs. 89 min, p = 0.825, and median 285 vs. 234 min, p = 0.154, respectively). PRT did not differ significantly between groups (median 53 vs. 48 min, p = 0.626). The proportion of patients achieving 90-day mRS 0-3 did not differ significantly between groups (45.5% vs. 50.0%, p = 0.692). No significant differences were observed in TICI 2b-3 (80.0% vs. 82.6%, p = 0.802) or sICH (3.6% vs. 4.3%, p = 1.000). In the multivariable logistic regression, younger age (odds ratio [OR] 0.922, p = 0.002) was an independent predictor of 90-day mRS 0-3, whereas off-hours status was not (OR 0.917, p = 0.845). CONCLUSION: Despite prolonged time from hospital arrival to treatment initiation in the off-hours group, the proportion of patients achieving 90-day mRS 0-3 did not differ significantly between groups. In multivariable logistic regression, younger age was an independent predictor of 90-day mRS 0-3. Further efforts are needed to identify the causes of off-hours delays and to improve our clinical care system.

title: Blood-Based Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease: Advances in Detection Technologies and Clinical Applications.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder. Irreversible pathological alterations are already present when clinical symptoms emerge. Therefore, early diagnosis and intervention are crucial for improving patient outcomes and reducing the social and healthcare burden. With its advantages of minimal invasiveness, convenience, affordability, and high accessibility, blood-based testing has overcome the limitations of conventional methods, becoming a major focus of research in early AD diagnosis in recent years. Based on the key domestic and international research findings in recent years, this paper systematically reviews the types, mechanisms of action, and relevant detection technologies of blood-based biomarkers for AD.

title: Impact of artificial intelligence-assisted health management on blood pressure and self-management efficacy in older adults with hypertension.
abstract: PURPOSE: This paper examined the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted health management on blood pressure control and self-management effectiveness in older adults with hypertension. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Two hundred hypertensive patients were randomly assigned to a usual care group (routine health management) or an intervention group (AI-assisted health management, including aspects such as intelligent monitoring, early warning and proactive intervention, among others) (n = 100 each). Primary outcomes included blood pressure control rate (<140/<90 mm Hg) and systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP and DBP). Secondary outcomes included improvement in lifestyle behaviors, level of hypertension knowledge awareness, self-management efficacy, medication beliefs, quality of life, and management satisfaction. RESULTS: Following one year intervention, the intervention group demonstrated a higher blood pressure control rate than the usual care group (88.66% vs. 64.89%), along with lower SBP (128.49 ± 6.63 vs. 135.38 ± 7.31 mmHg) and DBP (77.49 ± 6.07 vs. 81.84 ± 5.44 mmHg) (all P < 0.05). Additionally, the intervention group showed superior improvements in smoking behavior change, alcohol consumption behavior change, low-salt and low-fat diet adherence, and regular exercise attainment, as well as higher scores on the Hypertension Knowledge-Level Scale, Hypertension Patient Self-Management Behavior Rating Scale, Modified Beliefs about Medicines Questionnaire, physical component summary and the mental component summary, and Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8 (all P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: AI-assisted health management enhances blood pressure control, and improves self-management capacity, quality of life, and service satisfaction in older adults with hypertension.

title: Diagnosis and management of thyroid cancer in adult patients. Recommendations of Polish Scientific Societies and the National Oncology Strategy, 2026 update.
abstract: The current update of the "Recommendations for the Management of Thyroid Cancer in Adult Patients" is based on a critical appraisalof whether the recommendations published in 2022 by the Polish Scientific Societies and the National Oncology Strategy remain valid,and which statements require modification or updating in light of the American Thyroid Association (ATA) Guidelines published in 2025. We have also taken into account the most recent National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommendations, as well as guidelines from other international and European scientific societies addressing thyroid cancer, adapting them to the specific epidemiologicaland legal conditions in Poland. We decided that the current Recommendations would not include management of medullary thyroid cancer, as, in our opinion, the Polish Guidelines published in 2022 and 2024 remain up to date. The Recommendations are divided into two sections: "General Principles" and "Clinical Management". The "General Principles" sectionoutlines the key principles of thyroid cancer management, whereas the "Clinical Management" section specifies these principlesaccording to the risk of recurrence, incorporating the well-established and highly accurate ATA 2025 risk stratification system. Thus,the reader will find specific management recommendations depending on whether the patient has low-risk or high-risk thyroid cancer. The "Clinical Management" section includes a dedicated subsection outlining the recommended clinical approach to thyroid noduleswith indeterminate cytology. In these Recommendations, the management of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma and thyroid lymphomas is addressed in a separate subsection. In addition, brief information on other rare histological subtypes of thyroid cancer is also provided.

title: Using the 4Cs of Primary Care to Ensure Timely Diagnosis of Alzheimer Disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Disease-modifying treatment is available for patients diagnosed with early symptomatic Alzheimer disease [AD, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and mild dementia]. Recognition and diagnosis of MCI and dementia occur every day in the primary care setting, but diagnostic challenges and delays are common. Over 90% of MCI cases are missed, and more than half of AD diagnoses occur when the disease is in the moderate or advanced stage, when crises and emergencies are more likely to occur. DISCUSSION: Diagnostic delays limit opportunities to organize and implement proactive, comprehensive patient care and treatment and to prepare individuals and caregivers for the long-term implications of progressive dementia. With the advent of new diagnostic methods, including blood-based biomarkers, AD can now be diagnosed with greater precision and ease at a lower cost. Given the expected increase in prevalence of AD in the next 2 decades and the growing shortage of geriatricians and memory disorders specialists, the role of the PCP in diagnosing AD will be of even greater importance. However, many PCPs do not feel confident or equipped to recognize and diagnose patients with early symptomatic AD. To empower PCPs as key participants in diagnosis, we propose an approach aligned with the fundamental strengths of primary care, codified in the 4Cs (first contact, comprehensiveness, coordination, and continuity of care). CONCLUSION: Using the 4Cs framework, PCPs can increase the rate of timely diagnosis of symptomatic AD and be afforded more time to provide comprehensive care, using proactive rather than reactive management strategies throughout the diagnostic process.

title: Tumor-Immune Microenvironment of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: Implications for Immune-Based Prevention and Therapy.
abstract: Early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC), typically defined as colorectal cancer diagnosed before 50 years of age, is increasing in incidence worldwide and exhibits distinctive clinical, molecular, and environmental features compared with later-onset (LOCRC) disease. However, the tumor-immune microenvironment (TiME) of EOCRC and its implications for prevention and therapy remain poorly characterized. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on the TiME of EOCRC and contrast it with that of conventional LOCRC. We first discuss global features of the EOCRC immune landscape, including innate and adaptive immune composition, functional states, and spatial organization, highlighting areas where apparent age-related differences reflect true biology versus confounding by tumor site, stage, or mismatch repair (MMR) status. We then examine immunogenomic and epigenomic determinants-such as MMR deficiency distribution, microbial mutational signatures, chromosomal instability, and age-conditioned methylation programs-that shape neoantigen landscapes, antigen presentation, and immune evasion in younger patients. Next, we review microbiome-driven immunomodulation, focusing on dysbiosis, genotoxic bacteria, and early-life and young-adult exposures as joint modifiers of mucosal immunity and tumor development. Finally, we explore how these insights inform immune-based prevention (risk stratification, screening, diet and microbiome interventions, and chemoprevention) and immunotherapy strategies, including checkpoint blockade and rational combinations in the predominant microsatellite-stable EOCRC population.

title: Outcomes of Chemoimmunotherapy in Metastatic Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Carcinoma: A Single-Center Clinicopathologic Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinomas (PanNECs) are a rare, aggressive subtype of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms. Based upon similarities to small cell lung cancer (SCLC), advanced PanNECs are commonly treated with platinum and etoposide chemotherapy; however, outcomes remain poor. Although first-line chemoimmunotherapy has improved survival in SCLC, its role in PanNEC is not well defined. METHODS: We report on a retrospective cohort of 13 patients with metastatic PanNEC treated at Memorial Sloan Kettering with either first-line combined chemoimmunotherapy or first-line chemotherapy alone. RESULTS: In the first-line metastatic setting, patients who received chemoimmunotherapy (N = 5) demonstrated longer median progression-free survival (17.0 months vs. 2.8 months, P = 0.002) and overall survival (31.0 months vs. 16.0 months, P = 0.031) compared with those who received chemotherapy alone (N = 8). In the second line or later setting, five patients received immunotherapy-containing regimens with a median progression free survival of only 3.0 months (95% confidence interval 1.4 months, Not Reached). Radiologic responses observed in patients receiving chemoimmunotherapy in the first-line metastatic setting were 2 complete responses and 3 partial responses. Germline variants included one patient with a BRCA2 mutation, one patient with co-existing BRCA2 and ATM mutations, and one patient with a MUTYH mutation. Exploratory genomic analyses showed common mutations in TP53, RB1, and KRAS, low tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite stability. Exploratory multiplex immunofluorescence demonstrated heterogenous immune cell infiltrates without a consistent biomarker pattern associated with response. CONCLUSION: In this single-center cohort, early incorporation of chemoimmunotherapy in PanNEC was associated with improved survival. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support prospective, multicenter evaluation of first-line chemoimmunotherapy strategies in PanNEC (SWOG S2012, NCT05058651) [1].

title: Multisystem Outcomes of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Versus Active Comparators in Type 2 Diabetes: A Multicenter Target Trial Emulation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multisystem effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) beyond cardiometabolic outcomes are incompletely characterized against active comparators in type 2 diabetes (T2D). We compared GLP-1RA with sulfonylureas (SUs), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP4is) in adults with T2D. METHOD: In a multicenter target trial emulation across 5 University of California academic medical centers (2012-2025) using harmonized electronic health record data, adults with T2D newly initiating GLP-1RA, SU, SGLT2i, or DPP4i were propensity score-matched 1-to-1 within site via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (>11 000 covariates), with up to 5-year follow-up. We screened 181 prespecified incident outcomes across 15 body systems, pooling hazard ratios by random-effects meta-analysis. Robustness required leave-one-medical-center-out stability, E-value ≥1.5, and false discovery rate-adjusted P < .10. RESULTS: Among 70 982 matched adults, 118 robust associations were identified (65 for reduced risk and 53 for increased risk). Risk reductions were most consistent for cardiovascular outcomes, including myocarditis/cardiomyopathy (summary hazard ratio, 0.38 [95% CI, 0.32-0.44] vs SGLT2i), acute myocardial infarction (0.53 [0.42-0.66]), heart failure (0.71 [0.58-0.88] vs DPP4i), and thromboembolism (0.69-0.72), and for nephritis/nephrosis (0.73 [0.67-0.79]), nutritional anemia (0.70-0.81), coagulation disorders (0.73-0.81), and tobacco-related disorders (0.60 [0.49-0.74]). Risk increases were found for musculoskeletal conditions (22 associations); osteoarthritis 1.48 (1.29-1.68), stress fractures 1.68 (1.15-2.47), diverticular disease (1.18-1.33), sleep-wake disorders (1.27-1.54), and menopausal disorders (1.32-1.52). CONCLUSIONS: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist initiation was associated with reduced cardiovascular, renal, hematologic, and tobacco-related risk, consistent with outcome trials. Increased risks for musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and sleep-wake disorders warrant monitoring as the clinical use of GLP-1RAs continues to expand.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

title: The Target48 Neurodegeneration panel: A novel tool for profiling protein signatures in neurodegenerative disorders.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Novel tools for absolute quantification of established and emerging fluid neuro-biomarkers are required to advance diagnostic studies and improve biological insights. METHODS: We conducted an extensive analytical and clinical validation of the OlinkTM Target 48 Neurodegeneration panel (T48 Neuropanel) in 352 paired cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma samples from cognitively unimpaired controls (CU), Alzheimer's dementia (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), n = 44 per group. Comparisons with benchmark assays were performed. RESULTS: Good detectability (CSF: 31 out of 42 assays; plasma: 38 out of 42 assays) and technical performance was observed. Benchmark assays showed good correlations, supporting transformation formula's. Next to emerging biomarkers (MMP10, ITGB2), discriminative performance was excellent in AD: CSF pTau217: area under the curve (AUC) = 1; FTD: plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL): AUC = 0.952; and DLB: CSF dopa decarboxylase (DDC): AUC = 0.901. DISCUSSION: This analytical and clinical validation of the T48 Neuropanel highlights initial cutoffs and emerging biomarkers to aid clinical studies for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

title: Physics-informed depth-enhanced surface tracking for cumulative dose reconstruction in breast radiotherapy: An in silico feasibility study.
abstract: PURPOSE: Surface guided radiotherapy (SGRT) provides nonionizing motion monitoring but lacks direct correlation with internal dosimetric changes. Purely data-driven models for surface-to-internal deformation prediction often yield biomechanically implausible results. This study proposes a physics-informed depth-enhanced (PIDE) framework, validated in silico, to reconstruct internal deformation and cumulative dose from noisy surface measurements. METHODS: A virtual clinical trial (VCT) was conducted using weekly cone-beam CT (CBCT) data from 29 breast cancer patients. We simulated consumer-grade RGB-D sensor noise ( σ ∝ z 2 ) on extracted patient surfaces. To map external surface features to internal deformation vector fields (DVF), we developed a regularized ridge regression model. Unlike traditional models, ours integrates a spectral energy penalty derived from patient-specific CBCT motion priors, constraining predictions to physically plausible deformations. Patient-specific clinical RTDOSE distributions and 348 anatomical landmarks were utilized to evaluate the dosimetric and geometric accuracy. Vector field smoothness was quantified using the Jacobian determinant. RESULTS: Under realistic simulated sensor noise, the PIDE framework achieved an anatomical target registration error (TRE) of 1.33 ± 1.42 mm (compared to an initial misalignment of 2.14 ± 2.38 mm, representing a 37.8% error reduction). The physics-constrained regression yielded an RMSE of 2.31 mm (r = 0.720) for motion prediction and effectively eliminated nonphysical tissue "folding" artifacts (reducing negative Jacobian voxels from 0.54% to 0.10%, p = 0.0209). Dosimetric evaluation using actual patient treatment plans achieved a mean Gamma passing rate (3%/3 mm) of 99.68 ± 0.30% (range: 99.00%-100.00%), with 100% of patients (29/29) exceeding the 90% clinical safety threshold. The end-to-end algorithmic inference latency was 2.71 ms per frame, demonstrating high computational efficiency. CONCLUSION: The integration of geometric surface features with patient-specific physical constraints successfully prevents nonphysiological deformation artifacts caused by sensor noise. This in silico study demonstrates the feasibility and computational efficiency of the PIDE framework for rapid cumulative dose monitoring.
journal: Journal of applied clinical medical physics

title: A collaborative quality improvement project to enhance knowledge of preventive health screening and services among new migrants and refugees in the Australian Capital Territory.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Language accessibility barriers of health information may limit health literacy, and reduce awareness of local services for culturally and linguistically diverse communities. As a result, culturally and linguistically diverse populations face challenges accessing preventive sexual and reproductive health and cancer screening services. The aim of this quality assurance and improvement project was to improve knowledge of key messages outlining when and how to access cervical, breast, and sexual health screening services. METHODS: A community-based quality assurance and improvement project delivered culturally sensitive, plain English health education sessions through Adult Migrant English Program classes in 2023. Education focused on key messages about when and how to access screening and care from BreastScreen ACT, Canberra Sexual Health Centre and Women's Health Service. Session effectiveness was assessed using matched pre-post session questionnaires. Median scores of percentages of correct answers on a student's questionnaire before and after intervention were compared using the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: Paired questionnaires were analysed for Canberra Sexual Health Centre (n = 29), BreastScreen ACT preliminary/level 1 (n = 75), BreastScreen ACT level 2/3 (n = 70) and Women's Health Service (n = 127). Median scores increased across all services apart from BreastScreen ACT preliminary/level 1 questionnaires, where there was a high baseline level of knowledge (median 100%). Feedback from Adult Migrant English Program teachers indicated the sessions were well-received. CONCLUSION: Delivering health education through trusted Adult Migrant English Program settings improved culturally and linguistically diverse participants' knowledge of key messages relating to sexual, cervical, and breast health screening and services. This replicable model strengthens health literacy and supports equitable access to preventive screening.

title: Oestrogen Receptor Positive Tall Cell Carcinoma With Reversed Polarity of the Breast: A Case Report of a Challenging Lesion on Core Needle Biopsy.
abstract: Tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity is a rare, low-grade breast carcinoma with variable morphology and a characteristic molecular profile. Diagnosis on core-needle biopsy is challenging due to architectural overlap with benign and low-grade papillary lesions. We report a 42-year-old woman with a right breast lump in whom this diagnosis was established on core-needle biopsy through integrated histological, immunohistochemical, and molecular assessment.
